title: Serious Sam: Shatterverse
description: Serious Sam: Shatterverse is a co-op roguelite FPS for 1 - 5 players. Blast through shifting universes, stack wild boons, bend the rules with run modifiers, and hunt Mental's deadliest forces. Fall fast. Come back louder.

segments.text: I played Serious Sam a fair bit throughout the years, and if there's one thing this series has shown me, it's that sometimes you don't need to fully reinvent the wheel. Give me a stupid arsenal of guns, several hundred screaming enemies heading in my general direction, some heavy metal music, and let me figure out the rest.

It's a formula so simple you'd think it'd be impossible to bugger it up and yet somehow Serious Sam Shatterverse has managed to do just that. Feeling like a game that takes about a dozen different concepts, flings them all at a wall and hopes something sticks. And while it's not a game that's like fundamentally broken or unable to function, it is something that feels like it doesn't understand what a Serious Sam game is supposed to be.

A big part of why that might be is probably because Croteam isn't actually the lead developer this time. It's instead been made by Behaviour Interactive, the same guys who created Dead by Daylight. Which is probably why this thing just doesn't feel like a Serious Sam game at all. But what is the whole thing about? Well, I'm so glad you asked. Let's just find out, shall we?

So the premise for this is that you're initially playing as, I guess, the original Sam, or at least a variant called Retro Sam, that's been pulled into the Shatterverse, which, yeah, is more or less like a multiverse, with this new uber-mental having messed up the barriers between all these different universes and caused them all to overlap and collapse, or something. But to be honest, I don't really know. I mean, the game gives you bugger-all exposition and just kind of throws you right into things without any real setup.

Whatever exposition or advancement to the plot there is, is usually just dialogue that occurs during gameplay. Usually when you're in the middle of combat with a bazillion enemies, where trying to focus on what people are talking about is damn near impossible. Honestly, the amount of times you're fighting for your life here and the characters are just yapping away in the background is too many times to count.

But I think it really just exists to be a justification for why you're running the same few looking worlds over and over, more than it is trying to be some kind of cohesive plot about Ubermental being Serious Sam's version of Doctor Doom. Either way though, a plot is more or less non-existent here, with this also just having terrible writing.

featuring some incredibly unfunny lines of dialogue, where characters try to make these offbeat remarks and jokes that just fall completely flat. Mostly when the different versions of Sam are commenting on what happens during gameplay.

Because modern games, it seems, just can't go 30 seconds without someone talking for the sake of talking. Oh yeah, and off the back of that, how many versions of Sam do you think they gave us to players? I mean, like, take a guess, if there's an infinite amount of universes where a version of Sam could exist, how many do you think are gonna make an appearance? Maybe 10? 15? Well, no, how about 5?

The one they seem to be pushing the most here being a female version, of course, named Orphan Sam, who even talks down to Retro Sam a fair bit, making jokes about how dumb and dated he is. Which is a great move, you know, insulting and ridiculing the guy who's carried the entire franchise. I mean, there's one bit where he just says a harmless throwaway line, and these new characters all start to act like they're gonna send him off to sensitivity training.

How about the fact that guy's been sidelined on his own title screen for his own game series? Put off to the side there while these new guys hog the show. But you know what? It's exactly the kind of thing I'd expect from the same game that redesigned the harpies to be covered up more. That actually leads me into one of the biggest things that really stuck out to me here, and that's just this generic cookie cutter art style.

Where it's like Serious Sam crossed with a free-to-play mobile game crossed with Fortnite. I mean just look at this title screen again and tell me it doesn't look like a Fortnite splash screen you'd see before the game loaded in. Not to mention it also feels like we've got Borderlands at home with the very Samster players having unique abilities, enemies also having levels and giant health bars, along with elemental effects for weapons like fire and frost. The bosses even spew out all their loot in a similar fashion when they're killed.

Then you got these giant comical damage numbers popping up on the screen during combat, and these overly animated effects for explosions that looks absolutely nothing in line with the rest of the series. It's like they watched someone else play Serious Sam 2, and then tried to recreate it from memory. And it all just feels like the PG-13 version of Serious Sam, the homogenized, free-to-play version you can access on your phone if you've got a Netflix account. Made to appeal to everyone, but not anyone specifically.

Plus the whole 80s and early 90s retro vibe is just completely off, with it having these 8-bit sound effects and references to stuff like floppy disks and old Commodore-era computers. Which I find odd, considering the series started in 2001, when Commodore computers were ancient history, and even floppy disks were pretty much on their way out. Can we also talk about how this game aesthetically looks worse off than the original game? I mean, just take a look at all the interior areas inside these tombs and pyramids, and look at how dull and flat they are.

There's no depth or interesting lighting and it's all just devoid of any kind of eye-catching elements. And now look at how these areas looked in the first game from back in 2001. Same thing too when you're outside in the desert and forest areas. I mean, just compare these to the same thing on a 20-something year old engine. And I just want to know, like, how did Croteam make a more visually appealing game 25 years earlier on an engine that could run on a shoebox?

That jungle biome is so foggy that you almost can't even see what's attacking you which is doubly an issue because you've got those arachnoids and their annoying ass chainguns which can just shred through you at any range and always seem to be just a bit too accurate One of the biomes is the clear homeworld which also showed up in Serious Sam 2 and you can see here again how it just lacks any charm or vibrancy like they just asked an AI prompt to replicate what an area looked like it made it worse and then they still use the result anyway

And yeah, like speaking of clears, have you noticed how a lot of these returning enemies just look kind of different now? Which I guess can be justified given that this thing is set in alternate universes, which does make sense that there'd be different variants and all that kind of stuff. But even that really kind of proves my point in how this thing has lost its identity. As for the actual gameplay side of things when it comes to the shooting, well look, I don't think Shatterverse is inherently bad. It's just that it feels so generic.

Every run is you're trying to save like a single universe with each universe broken down into nine areas with three areas for each biome with the third area always ending in a boss fight with every kill you're earning xp and then after a certain amount you level up and you're able to choose from one of three intel discs giving you buffs like increased weapon damage maximum armor or even like a basic kill streak where as long as you keep the kills coming you'll get a faster firing rate or a reload time on your weapons stuff like that

Honestly, it's not super deep, it's just got a lot of basic improvements that make you slightly more powerful, with the level cap weirdly being set to only 10. Sam's also got a dash move, a double jump, and can use grapple points sporadically now too. With the bosses really being the main thing that's going to dictate how easy or hard your run is going to be, considering some of these are considerably more challenging than others. A boss like the Giant Lava Golem is pretty piss easy once you figure out its basic patterns.

But bosses like the giant Clear God and an evil version of Sam who's given off total Wesker vibes from Resident Evil can be a bit more of a problem. Simply because the Clear God has some really damaging attacks that aren't always clearly communicated to the player and Wesker Sam likes to hang back and spawn in a bunch of kamikaze beheaded. Either way though, at the end of each area you get a quick breather, you can upgrade Sam's ability and also purchase weapons and more upgrades.

And with the bosses, they usually drop a good chunk of extra loot and resources for you to collect. The problem is that a lot of this is heavily dependent on what weapons you're actually using. Given the game's whole RNG roguelite system, with almost all of Sam's iconic arsenal needing to be unlocked first, with earned resources before you can even use them. You start off with only a Desert Eagle, Shotgun, and Tommy Gun unlocked, with the game always letting you pick from one of these in a weapon chest at the beginning of each run.

All of the weapons have unlimited ammo, though they still need to be reloaded, and then some of the more powerful ones like the minigun or the laser rifle have an overheating system. Whereabouts all you can do is simply swap out to something else until they've cooled off. Then from that point on you play and explore the level, with better guns hopefully dropping and appearing, but only if you've unlocked them through an armory in the main menu. And I just feel like this idea alone fundamentally misunderstands what Serious Sam is all about.

I mean, all of the weapons in the original game really were designed with certain enemy types in mind. The revolver and the basic shotgun, for instance, were perfect against the weaker enemies like the Nars or the Beheaded. The coach gun was awesome against tougher enemies like the werebulls and the clears. Whereas stuff like the tommy gun and the laser rifle were great for enemies at range like the harpies and the arachnoids. And the original games generally gave you these weapons around the same time you started encountering enemy combinations where they became useful.

It's not rocket science. But when you're missing 90% of these guns, but still coming up against 100% of these enemies, and your loadout is only a basic shotgun or a desert eagle, well, it just completely fucking misses the point of what Croteam were going for when they designed that combat loop. I mean, you wanna know how much fun it is trying to kill an elite wereble with only a desert eagle? Well, I'll tell you, man, it's about as much fun as catching a cricket ball with your nutsack. This is ridiculous, though.

Eventually, you do start finding better tiers for weapons, which gives them improved stats for firing rates and damage, but those initial drops are almost always gonna be terrible. And you're still gonna have no control over what you're gonna get, and just hope you're lucky enough to get better options. Not to mention, almost all of the guns have really bad bullet spread, making it tricky to hit enemies from a distance. Because yeah, that's totally something we needed in a PvE game, isn't it?

Like, why does there need to be a weapon spread as a stat in a single-player and PvE-focused arena-style shooter? Like, are they trying to keep the gameplay balanced for the AI or something? Yeah, maybe they should have applied that bullet spread to the arachnoids. It's all just very RNG-based, where a run really only goes as well as the randomization lets it. Sometimes you'll get a decent weapon early on, but then other times you simply won't.

Making you realize how it's really not so much about skill a lot of the time, as it is just hoping the game's nice enough to give you a decent gun. It's also kind of funny how stupid some of the enemies are now, and I know that the lineup of bad guys in this Serious Sam games haven't exactly been Mensa candidates, but some of these guys really are quite stupid. And a lot of the times enemies just spawn in right on top of each other, where you can just hold down the fire button and wipe them out before they've even tasted fresh air.

The other factor that comes into it is the different versions of Sam you can play as, with each of these guys having their own unique personalities, but also their own unique abilities. And the way it works is that after a certain amount of kills, you charge up an ultimate that you can then activate, pretty much all of which just do a shitload of damage in a really small time. Retro Sam, for instance, can spawn in all these holographic clones that fire at enemies, sucks them in, and then explodes.

Orphan Sam can put out like a vortex of blades that sucks enemies in and then explodes. Creative. And then cartoon Sam turns himself into like a human cannonball and blasts everything around him. At the end of each area, you can choose from one or three upgrades for that ability. And while they do have different base modifiers, the Ultimates themselves mostly just boil down to giving you this quick burst of damage.

And I just never found anything approaching like clearly defined healer or support roles. Broken Sam, for instance, his ability is a giant laser blast that comes out of his hands. And one of the upgrades for it makes it so that it heals him whenever he uses it. No one else, just him. So it's really just your press Q to win button. You've got three tiers or modes all up here, which I guess more or less equates the difficulties with Serious, Mental and then Shattered. The thing is, the only one you can play through in the beginning is Serious.

Having to beat that one first before you can then move on to Mental. We're on Mental, you can then set off on this bold new challenge, playing through the exact same biomes you've already played, only this time with slightly more difficult enemies. Before you then beat that mode and unlock Shattered, where you then just replay through the exact same biomes all over again. Yeah, because as it turns out, there's only about six of these all up. Huh. Guess the multiverse ain't all that big.

The only real difference in Shattered is that the enemies are now ridiculously spongy. Because, yeah, that's how you make a game challenging. You just give the enemies an absurd amount of hit points. With the bosses also never able to melt your entire health off in a single blast.

Honestly, the jump in difficulty in this mode is just absurd. Like, it genuinely feels like no one playtested this at all. Especially considering how Serious and Mental tier were piss easy in comparison. To put it into perspective, it's like playing on Shattered is essentially starting a new playthrough, only you're suddenly jumping to the endgame, with dozens of enemies spawning in to attack you at once, all while you've only got a Desert Eagle or a shotgun. And it's almost like it's at the point where they want you to go back in and spend time grinding out resources to even really stand a chance at surviving.

There is a bit of a sense of that early on too, like where the game just wants you to die over and over, until you've at least unlocked a few of the basic weapons. On that note too, I did test out co-op mode a fair bit, and this seems to be horribly balanced, where it seems to buff up the boss's health points when you've got more people playing, to the point that we kept wiping on the first boss of every single run, because we just weren't doing enough damage and the boss was just incredibly spongy.

Despite it all being procedurally shifting and all that stuff, you'll also see some recurring rooms that are just awful to play through, such as this one that I like to call the Run Ender, a tall circular room with a giant spinning laser that also spawns in kamikaze enemies from all directions, preventing you from changing your direction to avoid them because of this insane damage this constantly spinning laser trap does.

The main thing these higher difficulty modes introduce is anomalies, where you can give the run negative modifiers for bonus resources. Like having to play through the game in a third-person mode the entire time, which is actually a bit of a benefit considering it gives you more situational awareness. Along with these challenge rooms, which are more or less like Shatterverse's version of Slayer Gates from Doom Eternal, but all of which you're gonna have seen and feel very familiar with after a couple of runs. The repetitive aspect of things I can-

Nothing beats the feeling of a good victory With almost every weapon and intel upgrade needing these things called catalyst orbs that are either dropped by enemies or just found in the environment randomly Along with that when you encounter a new enemy type for the first time a new boss or explore a new biome the information for that is unlocked in a codex back at the main menu

And then after completing a mini challenge from it, you can earn a few orbs from claiming these as well. And it might sound like a fine enough system, only everything you need to unlock is connected to this resource. From all the various weapons, the playable Sams, and then finally improving all of the Intel disc to increase their effects. The problem is that the amount that this all costs far outweighs the amount you come across. Unlocking weapons, for instance, can cost upwards of a hundred orbs.

And you can't simply save up for the one gun you want, because you have to unlock every preceding gun beforehand. To get the laser gun, for instance, I first had to unlock the sniper rifle and then the minigun, both of which cost around 150 or so orbs. And yes, totally what I think of when it comes to a Serious Sam game, having to grind resources just to be able to use the minigun. Each playable Sam costs 35 orbs to unlock, and then the various Intel discs can also cost similar to upgrade, with some of these having like four or five different tiers.

And now consider you really only get about 50 to maybe 60 orbs per run. And that's if you do an entire playthrough and make it through to the end, wiping out all of the bosses. And I don't know about you guys, but to me, that just sounds like an absolutely insane amount of stuff to have to collect. I get that they're probably trying to do this to keep people invested and make them play for longer, but it's the kind of thing where people are just gonna find a way to exploit the game and uncover a quick and easy way to farm these orbs.

And even then, like, you're dropping all of this stuff into upgrades, which don't even offer up all that much of a benefit. Like, look at this shit, upgrading lifesteal so it has a 20% chance to inflict bleed, which then has a 9% chance to give me back 5 health points. Wow! The best bonuses you get here don't even really come from the intel anyway, they actually come from trinkets. Specifically, equipping multiple types of a single trinket category. For instance, if you've got two of a certain kind, you get a 25% extra chance for a critical hit.

But you put that up to four trinkets and it now becomes 60%. Plus a lot of these trinkets really are the closest thing we get to actual perma upgrades. It's just a shame that, again, upgrading these is so expensive, with the player having to constantly disassemble the trash ones they find to earn the resources. Not to mention you still need the weapons and upgrades you've unlocked to actually drop during a run, which isn't always going to be a definite thing.

That starting chest, like I said, always gives you a pistol, a shotgun and a tommy gun, but whatever else you find outside of that is just down to chance. And I didn't even see a minigun drop until like four or five runs after I'd unlocked it. So it's like even if you spend all these resources buying something, it's not even guaranteed to show up. And then when it does finally show up, it ends up being crappy and a low tier. But the thing that pisses me off the most here is the way this game handles health.

And this right here, I genuinely think might be one of the worst designed health systems in an FPS I've played in recent memory. Because for some reason they thought it would be a good idea to make healing items more or less non-existent on the higher tiers. Where outside of vending machines in between areas, the main way to get your health back is through executing enemies. Kinda like how you could finish off enemies in Serious Sam 3, only now it's been integrated as an essential feature, which doesn't work for a bunch of reasons.

For starters, it's often tricky to keep track of how much health enemies even have left when you got like a dozen of them coming at you at once. Plus, it's really easy to accidentally kill them when you're trying to get them low enough for the execution. Oh, yeah, and if you want another example of just how clueless this game is, they let you execute the kamikaze enemies. Like, just think about that for a second. More than that though, the amount of health you get back from this is absolutely useless and it even gets less and less for each tier.

Serious for instance, you get back 15, on Mental it's 10, and then on Shattered it's only 5. You'd think too that maybe like the big enemies would drop more health points, like maybe the werebulls or the giant lava golems, but no, they dropped the same amount as everyone else.

And it'd be like, imagine playing Doom Eternal, right? And you're doing your nightmare run, and you glory kill a tyrant, and you get back, you know, five or ten health points. It wouldn't make sense there, so try and make it make sense here. Or am I actually supposed to spend five minutes going around executing 20 enemies until I get my health back? Was that the plan? And yes, I know that Serious Sam 3 had executions too, but the key difference is that in that game, healing items were plastered all over the place.

They weren't treated like the Ark of the Covenant and barely seen like it is in Shatterverse You'd think that maybe you could upgrade this so that finishes give you more health, but no you can't And the closest you get is an upgrade that when maxed out gives it a 30% chance for enemies to drop more health on an execution And there's not even any kind of unique animations for this stuff either, it's just the same punch used every time

There are also like a lot of other minor annoyances, not massive things, but just the stuff you notice in games like this where you interact with mechanics so frequently. Like how every time you return to HQ after a run, the text that tells you you've just cleared the area covers the pop-up that shows what each Intel disc does. So you have to wait a few seconds for it to fade away.

Or like how when choosing an upgrade when you level up, it just takes that second or so longer than it should to let you get out of the menu and back into the gameplay. Again, small things, not massive deal breakers, just the kind of stuff that starts out like a splinter before it ends up feeling like a rusty piece of metal that's gone gangrenous. It all just kind of made me think about Siberian Mayhem and how a team of like eight people somehow made a better Serious Sam game than a company like Behaviour Interactive with their over 1300 employees.

And it's like they had that many heads cracking together, and this is what they came up with. Why do you use strange noises? Overall, Shadowverse is one of those instances where it's not that it's a bad game outright, but it is a bad Serious Sam game. A distinct element of sulfur. Oh, sorry.

And I just can't imagine that this is the sort of thing that hardcore fans of the series have really been pining for. I'm not even a hardcore Serious Sam fan and I was disappointed. And I guess I just don't really see the point of making a new game in a series that's long been established of having a certain gameplay style to suddenly come in and just take it in a completely new direction that no one asked for. Also by developers have had next to nothing to do with the series up until now.

And it honestly wouldn't have surprised me if this started out as something else, only someone just decided to whack the Serious Sam label on it and call it a day. It does have its moments, few as those may be, where it all feels like it comes together as the stars align and you get a decent roster of guns and abilities. But you shouldn't have to try this hard to have a fun time in a game like this. I'm sure in the future they'll put out some DLC, maybe a new Sam to players and daily events or stuff like that. But I just can't see people playing for that long for it all to matter.
Serious Sam fans have been asking for a new game for years now and I'm just so sorry it had to be this one
